# Ostrich 0.9 compression benchmark (project wiki, March 2026)

Ostrich compressed our sample of application text logs 4.1 times on average (zstd level 3: 3.2 times), at 410 MB/s
on one core.

Scope: the sample held 2,000 text log files, each under 1 MB. Binary payloads, files over 1 MB and multi-core runs
were not tested, so these numbers say nothing about them.

final.result:
Probably not. Nothing we have on Ostrich covers your data.

- **Your data:** The archives are protobuf binary frames, 40–300 MB per file.
- **The benchmark:** It only tested text logs under 1 MB. It says outright that binary payloads and files over 1 MB weren't tested, so the 4.1× ratio and 410 MB/s don't apply to your archives.
- **The readme:** It describes Ostrich as a dictionary compressor for small text records. Large binary files aren't what it's built for. It also needs a trained dictionary per stream, and the same dictionary to decompress. That means every archive depends on a dictionary you'd have to version and keep.

zstd is the safer default for these files. To test Ostrich anyway, benchmark it against zstd on a few real nightly files first, and compare ratio, speed and the dictionary overhead.
